title: The Bookbinder Who Bound His Own Way In
author: Robert Greene
wiifm: Yesterday Ericsson timed practice with a stopwatch. Today Robert Greene stretches the same question over a whole working life. We follow two lives side by side: Greene's own, a drifter through dozens of jobs who found his calling in his late thirties, and Michael Faraday's, a blacksmith's son who talked his way into science with a book he bound himself. Along the way you will learn the three stages of an apprenticeship, what a mentor is really for, why the best mentors eventually turn on you, and how much of Greene's method survives a hard look at his evidence.

b: Robert Greene was born in Los Angeles in 1959. As a boy he loved stories, especially the Greek myths and the history of the ancient world, and he went on to study classics, finishing his degree at the University of Wisconsin. After that, by his own account, he wandered.

He has said he worked something like eighty jobs. He was a construction labourer, a hotel receptionist, a translator, a journalist, an editor at Esquire magazine and a writer in Hollywood, among much else. He lived in London, Paris and Barcelona. To his parents, and often to himself, it looked like a man who could not settle.

In 1995, aged thirty-six, he was working at an art and communications school called Fabrica, near Treviso in Italy, when he met a Dutch book packager named Joost Elffers. Greene talked about the power games he had watched in every office he had passed through. Elffers asked if he had a book in him. The result, in 1998, was The 48 Laws of Power, a bestseller that made his name.

Looking back, Greene decided that the wandering had not been wasted at all. Every job had been an apprenticeship in watching people, and every subject he had loved as a child had pointed the same way. That idea, that a life only looks random from the inside, became the starting point of Mastery, published in 2012. To test it he went looking for the lives of masters, and the one he returns to most is a poor boy from south London.
ch.cap: Greene drifts through eighty jobs and cities, no plan

b: Michael Faraday was born in 1791 in Newington Butts, south London, the son of a blacksmith. There was no money and little schooling. In 1805, at fourteen, he was apprenticed to George Riebau, a bookbinder with a shop on Blandford Street. The work was glue, thread and pressing, seven years of it.

But a bookbinder handles books, and Faraday read the ones that passed through his hands. He read Jane Marcet's Conversations on Chemistry. He read the Encyclopaedia Britannica's long article on electricity. He began repeating experiments at the back of the shop with bottles and scrap wire.

Greene's first claim is built on lives like this. Each of us, he argues, has a Life's Task, an inclination that shows itself early and specifically, before anyone is paying us. Faraday was drawn to force and matter. Charles Darwin, whose exasperated father told him he cared for nothing but shooting, dogs and rat-catching, collected beetles, and at twenty-two sailed on the Beagle for five years of collecting and noticing.

Most people, Greene says, lose this pull. They replace it with what he calls a false self, a career built from other people's expectations, money and whatever path was open at twenty-two. It is not a dramatic failure. It is competent and well paid and faintly dead. His remedy is practical: go back to what drew you before you were strategic about it, look for a narrow niche rather than a crowded field, and do not simply take the path that pays best early.
ch.cap: Young Faraday reads the books he binds by candlelight

b: In 1812 a customer of Riebau's, William Dance, gave Faraday tickets to hear the celebrated chemist Humphry Davy lecture at the Royal Institution. Faraday took careful notes, hundreds of pages with diagrams. Then he did the thing that changed his life. He bound them into a handsome volume, in the only craft he had, and sent them to Davy with a request for any position at all. In March 1813 Davy took him on as a chemical assistant. Faraday was twenty-one.

Greene divides the apprenticeship that follows into three stages, and insists on their order. The first is Deep Observation, and it is passive on purpose. Your instinct in a new place is to impress. Greene says that is exactly wrong. You are there to learn two sets of rules: the explicit ones about how the work is done, and the unwritten ones about how power really moves, who defers to whom, which mistakes are forgiven, what gets someone quietly frozen out.

Those two sets of rules are rarely the same, and only the first is written down. Every workplace rewards something, and newcomers guess what it is from the job description and guess wrong. Observers work it out from who gets promoted and who gets ignored. Anyone who has started a new ward or a new job will recognise the truth of this. A few months of watching buys you a map most of your peers never draw, because they were too busy performing to look.
ch.cap: Faraday takes notes as Davy dazzles the Royal Institution

b: The second stage is Skills Acquisition, and Greene's advice is narrower than the modern instinct. Master one foundational skill properly before adding others. Expect the early stage to be tedious, because tedium is what practice feels like from the inside while the skill is being laid down. The reward comes later, and suddenly, when the skill goes automatic and becomes the floor you stand on to see further.

His model here is Benjamin Franklin. Apprenticed at twelve to his older brother James's printing shop in Boston, Franklin taught himself to write by taking essays from the Spectator, setting them aside, rewriting them from memory and then comparing his version with the original to see where he fell short. In 1722, at sixteen, he slipped letters under the shop door at night signed Silence Dogood, a fictional widow, because his brother would not have printed anything under Ben's own name. James published them.

On how to practise, Greene is specific. Two or three hours of intense focus will take you further than eight hours of the scattered kind. The work is not the hours. It is the attention, which is exactly what Ericsson found in the Berlin violinists.

He also tells you to value learning over money in these years. The reasoning is not moral. A job that pays more and teaches less trades growing capital for cash, and at twenty-five the growth is worth far more than the cash. By forty the trade runs the other way, which is why it has to be made early.
ch.cap: Young Franklin slips Silence Dogood under the print-shop door

b: Greene thinks the mentor relationship is the most efficient learning technology humans have, and his reasons are mechanical rather than sentimental. A mentor narrows your attention to what matters now, cutting years off the search. And a mentor gives you fast, specific feedback on your actual work, which no book or video can do. You can learn a lot from someone's published output, but it cannot correct you.

Faraday's mentor came with a price. In October 1813 Davy set off on a long tour of Europe, and took Faraday as his assistant. Davy's valet had refused to go, so Faraday was asked to act as valet as well, and for around eighteen months he was treated by Lady Davy as a servant. He carried the luggage. He also met the great scientists of France and Italy, watched Davy work on a newly discovered element in Paris, and came home in 1815 with a scientific education no English university could have given him.

Greene's advice on choosing a mentor is unsentimental. Choose for what you need at this stage, not for prestige. Prefer the one who will tell you plainly that the work is poor. Absorb the method, not the mannerisms. And expect, eventually, to push back.

Faraday's eighteen months as a servant look humiliating from the outside, and he wrote home that he sometimes thought of giving it all up. But Greene reads the choice as strategy. Faraday had worked out what he needed, which was proximity to the best chemist in Europe and a front-row seat at his work, and he was willing to pay for it in pride. Most people, Greene suggests, would have walked out at the first insult and kept their dignity and lost the education.
ch.cap: Faraday rides with the luggage on Davy's European tour

b: The dark half of the mentor story is the one people skip. In 1821 Faraday showed that a wire carrying a current could be made to rotate continuously around a magnet, the first electric motor in principle. He published without crediting the work of William Wollaston, and was accused of taking Wollaston's ideas. Davy sided against him.

In 1824, when Faraday was proposed as a Fellow of the Royal Society, Davy was its President and opposed the election. Faraday was elected with a single vote against him. It has long been assumed that the vote was Davy's, though a secret ballot means nobody can prove it. The pupil had outgrown the master, and the master did not enjoy it.

Greene's instruction is to see this coming. Take what you need without resentment, and leave before the relationship becomes a ceiling. Faraday did exactly that. He stayed loyal in public, never attacked Davy, and quietly built his own reputation. Davy is said to have remarked late in life that his greatest discovery was Michael Faraday, though like many good lines it is hard to source.
ch.cap: One black ball falls as Faraday joins the Royal Society

b: Greene spent years before Mastery writing about power, and the book's chapter on social intelligence carries that history. Social intelligence, in his sense, is not charm. It is the discipline of seeing people as they really are rather than as your hopes or grudges paint them. Idealising a colleague and demonising one are the same mistake in opposite directions, and both waste energy you need for the work.
The method is to weigh behaviour over words and pattern over single incidents. Watch what someone does repeatedly, across situations and over months. Notice tone, timing and what they avoid saying.

He names seven recurring types to recognise, which he calls the Seven Deadly Realities: envy, conformism, rigidity, self-obsession, laziness, flightiness and passive aggression. The useful point is that each is triggered by something you can control. Envy is provoked by showing off your advantages, so let the work speak. Rigidity is provoked by frontal challenge, so present change as continuity. The aim is not manipulation. It is to stop generating friction you do not need while you are trying to build something.
ch.cap: Behind the smiling masks, behaviour tells the truth

b: The third stage of apprenticeship is Experimentation: taking on work just beyond your competence and showing it to the world while mistakes are still cheap. Beyond that lies what Greene calls the creative-active phase, when your skills are solid enough to reshape the rules rather than follow them. In 1831, after years of patient work, Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction, the principle behind every generator that now lights our homes.

Greene offers three techniques worth stealing. The first is negative capability, a phrase from the poet John Keats: the ability to stay with doubt and contradiction without grabbing the first available answer. Many bad decisions are simply premature closure. The second is to keep a notebook by the bed, because the loose mind on the edge of sleep makes connections the deliberate mind will not, and they vanish within minutes.

The third, and the best, is to treat anomalies as treasure. The result that does not fit is not noise. It is the only place a new idea can come from. The neuroscientist V. S. Ramachandran took the odd phenomenon of phantom limb pain seriously, devised a simple mirror box to relieve it, and changed how we think about the brain's map of the body.

Against this Greene sets the traps that end careers just as they should open up: complacency, conservatism, dependency, impatience, grandiosity and inflexibility. Notice that most of these are diseases of people who have already succeeded.
ch.cap: Faraday's iron ring makes the needle jump: induction

b: What mastery looks like from inside, Greene says, is a change in perception. The master stops seeing parts and senses the whole, the way a chess master sees shapes rather than pieces. Greene calls this intuition, a compressed judgement built from years of immersion, and it is why masters often cannot explain their decisions.

His most vivid example is Temple Grandin. Diagnosed with autism as a child, at a time when institutional care was often advised, she thinks in pictures rather than words. When she began working on livestock handling, she did what the engineers at their desks had not. She got down on her hands and knees and crawled through the chutes to see what a steer sees: a coat flapping on a fence, a shadow across the floor, a shine on water that looks like a hole. Those details were making cattle panic. The curved handling systems she designed from that viewpoint are now used for a very large share of cattle in North America.

This is Ericsson's mental representation seen from the outside. It is the experienced nurse sensing that something is wrong before the observations change. It comes, Greene argues, from years of immersion, not from theory at a distance.
ch.cap: Grandin crawls the chute to see what cattle see

b: Greene's own career seems to support his thesis. The drifter with eighty jobs became, in his forties and fifties, one of the most widely read writers on strategy alive. In 2018 he suffered a serious stroke and spent a long time relearning how to walk, and has continued to write.

But the book's evidence has a structural weakness. Greene studies people who succeeded and reads the pattern backwards. There is no control group of equally patient, observant apprentices who served the same ten years under good mentors and stayed ordinary, though they certainly existed in large numbers. That is survivorship bias, and it is built into the method. His figures of ten to twenty thousand hours also inherit every problem in the practice research you met yesterday.

What survives is still substantial. The sequence of apprenticeship, then independence, is how law, medicine, nursing, trades and kitchens have organised themselves for centuries. His advice on mentors is concrete and usable. And his insistence on reading people by their behaviour over time is simply correct. Read Greene as a shrewd observer of how careers unfold, not as a scientist.

Faraday died in 1867, having twice turned down the presidency of the Royal Society that had once voted against him. He never had a university education. He had a bookbinder's bench, a mentor who made him carry the bags, and the patience to serve his apprenticeship to the end.
ch.cap: Faraday's bench at dawn; the unseen apprentices fade

take: What pulled at you before money was involved is cheap data about where your attention runs deep. Treat it as a hypothesis to test, not a destiny.
In any new team, spend the first months mapping who holds real power and which mistakes are forgiven. The written rules and the real rewards are never the same.
Add a second skill only when the first has gone automatic. Breadth before depth produces someone who cannot do anything hard.
Two intense hours beat eight scattered ones
Block the first two hours of the day, before email, for the one skill that decides whether your business is good, and defend them like a client meeting.
Put work in front of real judgement while mistakes are cheap. Polishing in private avoids the only information that matters.
Their value is narrowing your attention and giving honest feedback. Choose one who will say the work is poor, and give a junior person that treatment yourself.
Expect the mentor to resent you
Davy made Faraday carry his bags and opposed his election. Take what you need without bitterness, and plan your exit before the relationship becomes a ceiling.
Anomalies are where new ideas live
The result that does not fit is the most valuable thing on your desk. Resist the urge to smooth it away.
recall: How did Faraday get his first job in science?

After hearing Humphry Davy lecture in 1812, he bound his own detailed lecture notes into a handsome book and sent them to Davy asking for any position. Davy hired him as a chemical assistant in March 1813.
Why does Greene put Deep Observation before any attempt to impress?

Every workplace has written rules about the work and unwritten rules about power, and only the first are written down. A newcomer who performs before observing spends credibility against rewards they have guessed wrong.
What two things does a mentor provide that a book cannot?
A mentor narrows your attention to what matters at your current stage, and gives fast, specific feedback on your actual work. Published material cannot correct you.
What happened between Faraday and Davy in 1824, and what lesson does Greene draw?

Davy, as President of the Royal Society, opposed Faraday's election, and Faraday was elected with one vote against, long assumed to be Davy's. Greene's lesson is that protégés outgrow mentors, so take what you need and leave before the relationship becomes a ceiling.
What is the main weakness in Greene's evidence?

He studies only people who succeeded and reads their patterns backwards, with no comparison group of equally diligent people who stayed ordinary. That survivorship bias means the book offers shrewd hypotheses rather than findings.
note: Greene's biography is from his own interviews and published profiles; the job count of around eighty is his own figure. Faraday's apprenticeship, the 1812 lectures, the European tour and the 1824 election are well documented, though Davy's casting the one adverse vote is assumption, not proof, and the line about Faraday being Davy's greatest discovery is poorly sourced. Grandin's share of North American cattle handling is commonly cited but hard to measure precisely.
words: A German word for fingertip feeling: an intuitive, almost physical sense of a situation that comes from long experience.

The error of drawing lessons only from those who succeeded, ignoring the many who did the same things and failed.

Greene recommends it as a defence against premature closure in the experimentation stage of a career.

biz: Debt Support Direct clients are often frightened, so a new adviser should not learn by performing on them. Use Greene's order. For the first fortnight they observe live calls and note both the explicit process and the unwritten rules: how experienced colleagues spot vulnerability, when they slow down, what they never say. Then they take calls with a senior listening, and each week one recorded call is reviewed against two named skills with plain, specific feedback. Measure time to independent sign-off and the quality score on vulnerability identification, not calls per hour.

Greene says the result that does not fit is the most valuable thing on your desk. In a lead business, anomalies get smoothed away as noise. Start a simple weekly log: a keyword or SEO page converting far better or worse than its neighbours, a lender that suddenly declines a type of case it used to accept, a cluster of WhatsApp enquiries at an odd hour, a campaign whose leads drop out at the same stage. Each Friday pick one and ask why. Share ad-related ones with Grok as questions, not instructions. Measure how many investigated anomalies led to a change worth keeping.
connects: Greene's insistence on seeing people as they really are rather than as you wish them to be descends directly from Machiavelli's preference for how people actually behave over how they ought to.
Rockefeller began as a sixteen-year-old assistant bookkeeper in Cleveland, a long apprenticeship in the numbers of trade before he built his own empire.
Greene's fingertip intuition is Ericsson's mental representation seen from the outside, a library of patterns built by years of immersion.
recap:
Robert Greene was born in Los Angeles in nineteen fifty-nine, studied the classics, and then drifted. By his own count he worked something like eighty jobs: labourer, receptionist, translator, journalist, Hollywood writer. In his late thirties, at a school in Italy, he met a book packager who asked if he had a book in him. The answer was The Forty-Eight Laws of Power. Looking back, Greene decided the wandering had been an apprenticeship in watching people. That idea, that a life only looks random from the inside, became Mastery.

His favourite example is Michael Faraday, a blacksmith's son apprenticed at fourteen to a London bookbinder. Faraday read the books he bound. When a customer gave him tickets to hear the great chemist Humphry Davy, he took careful notes, bound them beautifully, and sent them to Davy asking for any job at all. At twenty-one he became Davy's assistant.

The first big idea is that early pulls are evidence. What drew you before money was involved tells you where your attention runs deep. Greene warns against the false self, a career built from other people's expectations, competent and well paid and faintly dead.

The second is that apprenticeship has an order. First you observe, quietly learning both the written rules and the unwritten ones about how power really moves. Then you master one skill past the point of boredom, the way Benjamin Franklin taught himself to write by rebuilding essays from memory. Then you experiment, showing work while mistakes are cheap.

The third is that mentors compress years, but at a price. Faraday toured Europe as Davy's assistant and also his valet, treated as a servant, and came home with an education no university could give. Later, when Faraday outshone him, Davy opposed his election to the Royal Society. Faraday was elected with one vote against, long assumed to be Davy's. Take what you need, Greene says, and leave before the mentor becomes a ceiling.

The fourth is that mastery feels like perception. Temple Grandin crawled through cattle chutes to see what a frightened animal sees, and redesigned an industry.

The honest caveat is survivorship bias. Greene studies the winners and reads the pattern backwards. There is no control group of patient apprentices who stayed ordinary. Read him as a shrewd observer, not a scientist.

Faraday never went to university, and twice refused to lead the society that once voted against him. He had a bookbinder's bench and the patience to finish his apprenticeship.

Serve the apprenticeship to the end, then outgrow it.
